sections.overview: The whale shark is the largest living fish, a slow-moving shark whose immense size comes with a specialised way of feeding on small prey. It ranges through tropical and warm-temperate seas, crossing ocean basins while repeatedly visiting some seasonal feeding sites.
sections.identification: Reliable body mass is not routinely measured for free-swimming whale sharks: even major aquariums note that weighing them accurately is very difficult. Length data are therefore more dependable than published mass estimates; the consulted sources provide no standard width or height. Its broad, flattened head bears a very wide mouth at the tip of the snout; five pairs of large gill slits open behind it. Pale spots and bars form a checkerboard over the dark back, and the pattern is distinctive enough for researchers to identify individuals in photographs. Individuals recorded at feeding sites often measure around 4–10 m, but this is an observation range that includes juveniles, and many coastal sites are dominated by young males. The 2025 IUCN assessment estimates male maturity at 6.8–9.2 m by region and female maturity at about 9–10 m. A Ningaloo re-sighting model estimated average eventual lengths—the limits approached as growth slows—of 8.5–9 m for males and 14.5 m for females; rare records approach 18 m, and these modelled averages are not maximum lengths.
sections.habitat: The species occurs in coastal waters and the open ocean, usually in warm seas, and spends much of its time near the surface. It can also dive into cold deep water; a satellite-tagged shark off Yucatán reached 1,928 m, although the purpose of such exceptional dives is not settled. Seasonal prey pulses bring sharks together at regional feeding sites, but their movements differ among regions and individuals.
sections.diet: Its food includes zooplankton such as copepods and sergestid shrimp, as well as fish eggs, larvae and small fish; the menu depends on what is locally abundant. In a feeding bout it may cruise with its mouth open, draw water in by suction, or feed nearly upright while stationary. Water exits through the gills after prey is retained by filtering pads in the pharynx. Motta and colleagues proposed that tangential cross-flow across the pad mesh may limit clogging, but described this as a mechanism rather than directly demonstrating that effect. Indirect biochemical evidence from tissues, faeces and prey at Ningaloo suggests floating Sargassum and its small associated animals can contribute to the diet there; this does not establish plant feeding as universal.
sections.behavior: At the northeastern Yucatán feeding area, hundreds of sharks gather in summer and disperse between August and October. A female tracked from Mexico travelled at least 7,213 km in 150 days. In Qatar, tracking showed that many tagged sharks returned to the same feeding area. Dives vary with region and prey: most tagged sharks spend much time in shallow water, yet some make deep excursions.
sections.reproduction: Reproduction remains poorly observed: the only confirmed pregnant female was a 10.6 m shark caught off Taiwan in 1995. She carried 304 embryos at different stages, including some still enclosed in egg cases and others already hatched; this showed aplacental yolk-sac viviparity, in which eggs hatch inside the mother and embryos develop without a placenta. The litter is an exceptional documented case, not a typical or known universal litter size. Newborns are rarely seen, so their birth size, nursery grounds and early growth in natural habitat remain uncertain.
sections.ecology: By filtering plankton and fish eggs, whale sharks feed on concentrated pulses of production and connect tiny prey to large marine predators. In the southern Gulf of California, seasonal plankton blooms draw juvenile sharks to feeding areas, where they can also become prey for large sharks and killer whales. Predation by killer whales is documented there: observations recorded four events of killing and consumption between 2018 and 2024, evidence that does not show orcas commonly hunt the species everywhere.
sections.conservation: Targeted fisheries once supplied meat, oil and fins, and some fisheries closed in the 1990s and 2000s; incidental capture in nets continues in parts of the range. The global IUCN assessment, assessed on 31 March 2025 and published in 2025, lists the species as Endangered and infers a 50–79% population reduction over three generations (120 years), with declines especially severe in the Indo-Pacific. Serious vessel strikes are another major threat because sharks cross shipping routes and aggregate predictably near the surface.
